review:
This game is awesome and totally addictive. Buy it now. 

The main gameplay loop consists of:
1. Find a house to steal from.
2. Watch the house with eyes/binoculars/hidden camera and find out how many people live there and when they are and are not home.
3. Find a route into their house watching out for pedestrians, cameras, alarms, and locked doors.
4. Skip over stealing their $10 vase and fill up on expensive ipads and antiques.
5. ???
6. Profit.

It's the type of game that you'll start playing on a whim one night and before you know it it's 3am and your rationalizing how if you just hit ONE more house you'd have enough to buy that lockpicking gun you've been eyeing.

This game totally stands as is but I'd have liked there to be some things in the game to spend your money on besides more tools for jobs as well as more houses who's items restock after a while. It might also be cool to experiment with different environments like breaking into highrise apartments or maybe a museum.

Thief Simulator starts out strong - it has pretty solid sneaking mechanics, and the idea is certainly not one you see around a lot - where the emphasis is on stealth and stealing stuff without it being detected, and getting away before the tenants notice. No combat, no assassinations - hurting people is actually a fail state - so its an interesting twist. As you unlock new tools and abilities you can try different entrances, which is all very fun.

... Problem is it kind of... starts out strong and doesn't go anywhere from there. Once you've completed the tutorial heists you've kind of seen it all. Find a way into the house, ideally while the tenants are out. Cram as much valuable crap per pound into your bag as you can. Maybe steal a few paintings or a flat screen TV, get out. Repeat. Repeat. Repeat. Once you've broken into one house you've kind of broken into them all.

Don't get me wrong, the tenants have different routines and sometimes tenants stay at home all day, and the layouts are different, but... the gameplay loop is always the same. The items you're stealing are generally the same. And you're only selling the stuff you steal so you can.. what? Buy expensive new equipment that lets you open a door that arbitrarily needs a better lockpick?

There's just not a lot of variety once you get past the initial tutorial, which is a shame. Its not a BAD game by any means - i'd rather give it a "middling" option if I could - but it IS thoroughly meh. Get it on sale, play it for an hour or two, then play something else and let your memories of it fade until you fancy playing it again. 

But hey, they're making a sequel, so maybe that'll be better.

[b][i]Thief Simulator[/i][/b] follows the story of the protagonist who is called The Thief. He begins his journey standing in someone's backyard, getting a call on his cell phone from a guy named Vinny who informs him he has been sprung from prison by a local crime gang that wants him to start thieving for them. Vinny also act as a tutorial and does a good job at it.

The game mechanics are good and the level of detail that has gone into all aspects of thievery - lockpicking, casing a house, breaking and entering, and stealth, just to name a few - is remarkable.

When it comes to gameplay, [b][i]Thief Simulator[/i][/b] is remarkably detailed and nuanced. This isn't Grand Theft Auto, so players can't just bungle a burglary and shoot up a building to escape - there is a certain finesse to the action, even while The Thief is driving around his beat up car and putting old electronics in the trunk to sell to a pawn shop.

[b]THE GOOD[/b]
- Vinny the tutorial guide your through the basic gameplay
- Sandbox mode works fine
- Great level of detail
- Nice graphics

[b]THE BAD[/b]
- Can get repetitive
- Almost too easy

[h1]8/10[/h1]

Another game in which I wish there was a Mixed Review option. I find it difficult to decide on whether or not I would recommend this game. To be honest, the screen shots for the game look way better than any moment I ever had while playing the game. I don't know what method they used to make it look so good, tidy things up, and add things in, but it is not representative of the final product.

The game itself is very ugly and bare bones. The different towns are sparsely decorated, trees and bushes and pretty much every asset is constantly reused, everywhere. Inside, and outside. There is rarely anything unique, other than the very few unique items to hunt and sell. The character models are just ugly, though the items inside the homes do look nice.

While not a lot of effort went into making the game world look good, the house designs/layouts are alright. Almost none of them repeat, only a few here and there. Most of the development time for this game seems to have gone in two places: house design, and the car dismemberment mechanics. There is more to disassembling a car than there is to picking locks levels one through three, disassembling jewelry, unlocking electronic devices, hot-wiring cars, disabling alarms, and hacking. All of those things are extremely simple, which is a real shame. Disassembling jewelry could have also been quite a good and fun mini-game, but it is just point and click. Either make it all fun and interesting, or don't make it take 30 minutes to fully disassemble a car.

But yeah, the house designs are well laid out. Tenant, and later guard, rotations are... interesting, and change for each home you visit. However, it doesn't make much sense a lot of the time. Where and when do some of these people sleep? They don't have that in their schedule. Why does a whole family sleep during the day? Why do some people never leave their home, ever? I can see they wanted different routines for each house, but it lacks realism. Also, I have never seen so many people walking in a neighborhood in my life. Both the upper class one, and the lower class one, and at night too! More people are walking around than live in both areas combined!

It feels like some people were assigned tasks, and none of them talked to each other. "You design the environments and people outside, you design the homes, you design the people inside and their schedules, you design what loot is inside the house", and so forth. That, or everything was all done in stages that didn't line up. Because a lot of the time, some of it does not mesh well, at all. Some homes, in order to actually loot the large items in them, you need to rely on exploits like throwing things out windows and over fences, when it is clearly not designed to do that. (Though honestly it should, why can't I pass paintings and flat screen TVs through fences? Why can't I set up areas to lower items down?)

Some places you have to use your car as a makeshift ramp to jump over properties, because the only way in and out is a single electronic door you cannot re-lock behind you that the tenants WILL see when they either leave or come home; and you do NOT have enough time to loot even a single item, because of the guard rotations. Some of it is just madness what you are expected to do, or how long you have to wait in closets, or how many times you have to go back in and wait in closets in a single heist.

If you could have time fast forward while in a closet, like you do while in your car in parking spots, that would be extremely helpful and way less time consuming. The fact that you can only pass time in your car in designated locations is also annoying. Another annoyance is that button prompts don't like coming up, especially for climbing windows or up pipes. When waiting and passing time in your car, there is no button to just start it up and drive. You have to exit your car, and get back in. There are so many little inconveniences like this that make the game annoying to play at times.

Unfortunately leveling up and getting skills does not make the game easier, or more fun. As you progress from poor neighborhoods and houses, to rich ones, you need more complicated gear and more complex methods to get in and out. The skill system and progression isn't there to make the game more fun, it is there to level lock you so you can't instantly go and rob rich people, which is a shame. If you can rely on your crowbar and your wits and still rob a heavily guarded home, that should be allowed. Also there is really no use to money other than buying more expensive gear to go with your new skills.

I did enjoy parts of this game though. There is just something about marking down the routines of the people on the property, finding cameras, making your way through all of the security, exploring the house and planning your routes. It is fun game-play, despite the game doing quite a lot to try and not make it fun by accident.

I think that is the perfect note to end on. This game is still fun, despite the many, many problems and issues that plague it. If you think you will have fun with this game, then I guess go for it. But, get it on sale. This does not feel like a $25 game with all of the bugs and issues. It regularly goes on sale for -85% off. Get it then if you are going to get it at all.

I really like the concept of this game, but I can't recommend it. 

Pros:-It feels fun to search through houses and unexpectedly find something valuable.
-The system of routines and secret vulnerabilities in houses is pretty cool
-The open-environment is really cool, and I like being able to just pick a house and rob it... However...

Cons:-The open-world is restricted by many factors, story, level ups, lack of gear... I would like if these things would help out in robbing a place, but most of the unlocks just basically unlock new houses... The glass cutter is about the only one I got that really feels useful in almost all houses, and then it gets ruined by window alarms later on. Also, every single time I've gone to a new house out of curiousity, it turns out I needed some new gear or level up to rob it.
-The AI is horrible, the cops constantly hit your car(even if it's parked far away from the house). Sometimes the cops will just pop into a room and instantly shoot you with the tazer through the wall. I had one case where a cop shot me from the third floor while I was on the first, because there was a small window where he could see me. It should be easier to outrun cops, to make up for poor AI they just had the cops instantly shoot you. The best way to avoid them is to hide in a closet, which can be boring if they take awhile to leave.
-Earning money doesn't feel useful until later on when you unlock a new house. Even then, I don't want to spend money on a house or furniture when I will eventually have to buy the next expensive upgrade to advance the "story"
-Also, when I say story, it really just feels like a game-long tutorial. Missions pop up and you either require new gear or level ups to do them, and they usually just involve stealing something from such and such house.
-Lastly, the big one for me is... While robbing houses is fun, when you need a level up you end up just robbing houses you've already been to and grabbing all the items that you've already got before... Going to new houses is kinda fun, but you just end up doing this for 75% of the game.
-The jobs usually just involve smashing something which ends up alerting everyone in the house.

I really wanted to like this game, it was fun for a little while. But I can't recommend it. I think it would be much more fun if they revamped the level up system, had you unlock only things that were helpful and not have to level 3 times just for the next story mission.

This game unfortunately misses almost all the important tenants of a good stealth game. While it does do some things right, like the lock-picking and scoping of the houses, it looks like it's trying really hard to be grand theft auto meets thief.

One major issue is the lack of a "caution" state. All too often you will find you're suddenly running for your life because old misses Powell noticed her bedroom wasn't locked and called the cops (who are already on her street). Something all stealth games need is a way to manage fail states, something that lets the player engage with the game even when they mess up. Most games do this by allowing the player time to prevent the alert; take out the witness, disable the alarm, or get out of dodge. 

As it stands there's no way to stop an alert, and the "caution" state lasts about as long as it takes to read "Burglary discovered by-" and then cops are here.

This wouldn't be so bad, but the game makes escape frustrating due to the lightning police response, and the one-hit capture. Not to mention the fact being spotted once drastically nerfs your rewards, it encourages players to save-scum rather than let the game play out. Personally I'd have liked to see a much more relaxed response; allow the player to understand what went wrong, figure out their escape, and weigh up if they can smash and grab anything on the way out. Right now you can either, run all the way to your car (the game punishes you for not parking your car in a parking lot), or sit in a dumpster for 5 minutes. 

It's hard to embrace failure in this game, and the issues of an imperfect design are made worse by punishing players for not meeting perfect requirements.

I'd love to see the devs take another crack at this because it's so close to a great stealth game.

While I like the concept and several of the elements of the game, I cannot recommend it as it stands. The more detailed explanation goes like this:

The game starts pretty strong. Skill progression can be slow at first, but it becomes less of a problem as you go, and while houses are somewhat similar (And there certainly is repetition as far as general layout of the house goes), there is enough changes to keep it fresh. 

While one of the strengths of the game is the possibility of having multiple approaches for each house, this only happens in the first third of the game. Given that the game allows/pushes you to master every skill, this element gradually disappears and you end up constantly being funneled into a single approach for every house.

This problem is compounded by the AI. Throughout the second half, the game starts adding increasing numbers of security guards who, unlike the tenants, are much bigger threat. Problem is, the AI is not up to par for either of them, but putting them as an active obstacle makes the issues all the more obvious. You can get constant notifications of being heard by the tenants/guards, but they do not react at all most of the time. Their field of view is always facing forwards (Even while making an idle animation in which they briefly look behind them) and they seem to have no peripheral vision whatsoever. In addition, their capacity for noticing burglarized items (e.g Open/Hacked doors) is inconsistent to the point I think the AI pretty much flips a coin when checking. This gets into straight up comedic territory when you realize that if you are standing in a roof or any place that cannot be accessed by walking, you are invulnerable, even when the guard is looking straight at you and knows you are there. Therefore, as you progress, particularly in the last third, the main strategy devolves into exploiting the AI glitches more than anything, which makes it rather immersion-breaking and all around unenjoyable. And don't even get me started on the uncanny ability of tasing you through literal walls.

Other questionable element is how big items are handled. As I understand, big items (Which are cumbersome to carry, can be seen by bystanders and you can only carry a limited amount in your vehicle) are a high risk-high reward alternative, which is balanced by their higher value compared to small items. Problem is, this is only true in the first neighborhood. From there onwards, the game proceeds to completely contradict this by reducing the value difference between both kinds of items (To the point of small items being worth more than large items in the lategame), increasing your carry capacity for small items (Which is obviously going to motivate you to go for small items) and placing security guards (That require you to be mobile, which you won't be if you are lugging a heavy item). I understand that the game was developed by a small team, and I'm willing to cut it some slack in the technical departments, but this is something inexcusable from a design perspective.
In addition, given that the average value of items grows by an order of magnitude between each stage; once you have all the thief tools, there is nothing else to buy (Other than furniture/wallpapers for your hideout, that are dirt cheap), so you end up quickly swamped with money and do not even have the incentive of actually doing the one thing you are supposed to be doing in this game, unless you want to do it for the challenge.

I really wanted to like this game, and I am willing to give another chance if the developers decide to make a sequel; but I can't recommend this one.

In its current state, I would not recommend it. As far as games go, this has more potential than any game I've played in years. Unfortunately, the story is very short and disappointing, there is no specialization. You are required to unlock basically every skill by the end of the storyline. And you hit a very noticable cap on your character's capabilities in the endgame. An increasing number of cameras and guards and a decreasing number of ways to enter the premises. Personally, I think the harder areas are more boring because there is a very linear way to complete them, unlike levels in the early and mid game, which allow multiple approaches.

As the game currently exists, it's about a man stealing small items or doing odd jobs in suburban neighborhoods, then improving his equipment and skills to steal cars, one-of-a-kind antiques, and doing painting heists. Unfortnately, it stops there.


-------------------------------------------------------

Good Things About the Game:
-Good save system; the moment you exit your car, you create a checkpoint. This makes it so there is no saving once you begin infiltration, so you can't use saves as a crutch. But you don't need to restart the whole thing. If you get caught, you're right outside the house, ready to break in again.
-The noise system is great
-The ability to mark and observe tenants and cameras to plan your path through the premises
-Pedestrian system adds some random elements to each playthrough


Bad Things About the Game:
-Agility is very underwhelming. You can't vault/climb walls, and vines and gutters (especially gutters) are very rare. You sometimes even get caught on ridiculous little curbs or sidewalk edges.
-Cars are finite, and it's honestly underwhelming that you need to learn a whole third of the whole skill tree just to steal two cars.
-Carrying large objects is extremely annoying and not rewarding. The houses with large objects worth looting have extremely advanced security, making it basically useless.
-Guards aren't distracted by things. Or at least not in a useful way. If they hear a door slam, they don't investigate it. They just call the damn police. It's really annoying, and being able to alter a guard's path would make a great addition to a stealth game like this
-Police are psychics, but stupid at the same time. If someone detects a burglary, but you're off the premises, they shouldn't be able to identify you if you're two houses away. Similarly, if a person notices their cameras are disabled, but you're on the next floor on an opposite wing of the house, police somehow know to run up to that exact room. If there's not a hiding spot, you're screwed. If there is, you have nothing to worry about.

-------------------------------------------------------


Personally, I think the absolute best way forward is to add various new mechanics and level layouts. Add rappelling, ziplines, temporary single camera jamming, drones, throwing distractions, or anything that adds to the flavor of being a thief. Suburban neighborhoods are nice, but adding some cat-burglar-like heists would continue the growth that the character experiences in the story.

I love this game so much, I really hope you continue to develop it and add more stuff to it. If there is dlc I would gladly pay for it (if its fair)

Thief Simulator is a mixed bag of a game. It's filled with really great ideas but held back by their low budget and some strange decisions.

[h1]What it does well:[/h1]
The game does a great job at making you feel like a common burglar. You can't just stroll into the first house you see and walk out with a fortune. Once you choose which house you want to rob, you have spend some time looking around from outside. Can you break the fence? Do they leave any windows open? Maybe you can climb a drain pipe and get in through the balcony. And where are the tenants? Do they ever leave the house empty? Can you get in when they're asleep?
Ok, so you planned everything and made it into the house. You can only carry so much weight, so you have to make sure you grab the most valuable stuff and hope it's not too heavy. That TV looks pricey, but you can't carry something so big in your backpack. Can you make it to your car with it before the tenants catch you and without attracting the attention of any pedestrians on the street?

That feeling is what this game does best. As you level up and get new skills you can carry more and get new tools but robbing a house never becomes a trivial task.

[h2]What leaves a lot to be desired:[/h2]
There's barely a story, but it somehow still manages to drag on. The AI is pretty bad and it often gets stuck preventing them from being where they should, which if it happens in the wrong place it can really screw you over. Your movement is limited, slow and clunky, and this game might feature the most pathetic jump in videogame history.

But by far my biggest issue with the game is the way it ranks up the challenge as you get into more difficult neighborhoods. It adds guards, more complicated house layouts, and less forgiving tenant schedules, which is all well and good. But then on top of that it starts taking options away from you. Certain tools like microcameras and glasscutters become completely pointless in the late game because instead of making them harder to utilize the game straight up stops giving you any chance to use them. You get new tools and skills, but you often end up restricted to just one or two ways of getting in or out of a house anyway, so instead of feeling like you're improving as a thief it just feels like you're barely keeping up.
A good stealth game should always prioritize giving the player as many options as possible to overcome any given challenge, and this is where Thief Simulator falls short.

[h3]Conclusion:[/h3]
Overall, it's a good but far from perfect game. Most of the issues with it are due to their low budget, which is perfectly understandable. In my opinion, it's very much worth it if you can get it relatively cheap.

After playing through the the main story three times, I can definitely say this game is worth the time and money you put into it. It can take a while to learn and understand some of the mechanics to the game, and you'll probably mess up many times before your "thieving skills" improve, but eventually you'll learn to develop a good system for each heist.

The game is visually decent, with some smooth daytime and nighttime cycles. Most of the objects that you can take will shimmer if you wave your flashlight in front of them. The character models are a little rough around the edges, but don't look too unrealistic. The neighborhoods and houses look great, especially the ones with more valuables inside them. Some textures/models could use a little polishing, but not too much.

The gameplay is pretty straight forward. You get assigned different objectives and missions to progress through the story, most of which involve doing a specific task in order to make money and level up. You can upgrade your equipment and thieving skills as you continue to progress through the game and unlock new things. A lot of back and fourth tedium can occur when it comes to driving back and fourth between the neighborhoods, hideouts, and the pawn shop. Remember to take breaks!

(Pro tip: Always look at the value of each object before taking it. You want to leave room for the good stuff.)

I really wish you had the ability to do more than just hide or run away from the police or surrounding residents when you get caught or set of an alarm. Having the ability to defend yourself by setting a trap or putting someone to sleep would've been a nice feature, and I believe both of these are coming in the sequel.

There's a lot more I can say about the game, but I think It's best to let people know what some of the basics are before buying and playing it. I can't wait for the farm and luxury houses to come as a part of the DLC, and I'm even more excited for the sequel when it releases! I hope this review was helpful to some.

Now that the Luxury Houses DLC is out, I'll be giving an update to my review. I won't go far into detail about each piece of content, but I'll briefly go over all three of them.

-The farming neighborhood and houses contract were a fun add-on to the game, and you can easily access them much earlier on in the main story, since you're only required to be level one to try them. (Just make sure you have the right tools when going in!) Stealing the tractors was my favorite part, and it gave a small breath of fresh air to have a new piece of scenery to explore.

-The "StolenGameZ" contract was a little boring. This is because the only thing you have to do for this contract is revisit a few houses from the first two neighborhoods you stole from, and steal a single video game box from each one. There's nothing more simple than that.

-The luxury houses are the star of the show. You get a second new neighborhood to steal from, and each house is well equipped with new levels of security, loot, and approaches for you to work with. You also get to purchase and learn new tools for this specific neighborhood.  Starting this contract definitely gives off the vibes of experiencing endgame content, as the houses are very difficult to navigate through, and have an extreme level of high risk and high reward value to each one. When I say they aren't easy, I'm not joking. There's a lot I can say about this part of the DLC, but I think foreshowing what you're getting yourself into can help motivate newcomers to try it out for themselves.

Furthermore, when I started the luxury houses contract, I saved and closed out my game to take a short break. When I returned back to load up my save, my profile was completely gone. This one's a toughie for me. Though I managed to get good mileage out of Thief Simulator (read: 13+ hours of gameplay) I can't in good conscience recommend buying it at full price. Even then I'm not sure how I feel about the final product. The gameplay is simple, repetitive, and plagued with bugs and issues that won't make you uninstall the game, per se, but it won't make you have any more fun.

I'm not going to go over the graphics because A) I rarely find them an integral part of the game and B) what you see in the footage is what you get. That being said, I think it's pretty telling when everything in the game looks like an asset bought from somewhere else. That's all I have on graphics--moving on.

Like the name of the game suggests, you play the titular 'Thief', a man of few words and a propensity for getting tazed. In debt to the Lombardi family, Thief needs to work off his debt by stealing a whole bunch of shit. That's basically all the story you're gonna get without spoilers. Using various tools such as the lockpick (a classic), the hacking laptop (which allows you to hack consoles from far away), and even a scuzzy van, you'll terrorize three neighborhoods in your quest for, in the parlance of our times, 'fat stackz'. You choose the time and means of ingress and egress, the homeowners choose how they're going to keep you out. As you progress you'll learn to monitor the schedules of your would-be 'thievees' and use this knowledge to break in and break out. On paper this is a pretty cool game, but what limits it is the execution of said game mechanics and the overall jankiness of the game itself.

To begin, I think I missed an opening FMV or detail in the manual where it explains how Thief is Batman's protegee or a cyborg following Asimov's Laws or something and can not, and WILL NOT, harm a human being. There's no way to knock someone out, tie them up, or really do anything to manage them. In fact, hitting anyone with a brick, crowbar, or a car (which happens much more often than you think) will result in a Mission Failure and force you to reload a checkpoint. This doesn't ruin the game, of course, but it makes what I'm about to describe a bit more irritating. If someone sees you doing your job, you have three options: 1) Stick around and get tazed like an idiot, 2) Run to the hills waving your arms like a maniac, or 3) Hide in a closet, somehow avoid police detection, and resume your looting. I've never tried it in real life, but I will admit hiding INSIDE a burgled house when the cops arrived is one of the most ballsy ideas I've ever heard. In this game it works 9 out of 10 times, so you might as well take the XP penalty and retreat to a magical closet. Don't go thinking you have it easy, though--the police have the best response time ever (clocking in to about 2 seconds) and they will follow you over hill and fucking DELL to shove a tazer up your orifices. Sometimes tenants pack them too! 

"Well okay," you might be huffing to yourself, "isn't that true of almost every stealth game?" You've got me there! However, Thief Simulator suffers from several bugs that, like I mentioned above, never really break your game, but do discourage you from playing it. Sometimes a guard will use psychic prediction and notice that you unlocked a door across the entire house. Sometimes guards and tenants will just throw their arms in the air, say "screw it" and teleport to another part of the house (read: your part of the house) because their AI lagged a little bit. Sometimes Thief's gout will act up and he won't be able to creep over a small piece of scenery such as a step on a stairwell or a bump on the ground. Sometimes even holding E to close something quietly will still slam the door/drawer/safe/car shut and alert everyone in the zip code. And SOMEtimes guards will channel John Wick and 360 Noscope you with a tazer from halfway across the map. 

In conclusion, these are all issues that can be ironed out. Maybe I'm a little spoiled after playing games like Thief, Splinter Cell, and Dishonored, but my philosophy is that if you're going to make a stealth game, it's IMPERATIVE that any error is a fault of the player's--not the game. If a player makes too much noise or drifts into an enemy's line of sight, fine! If said enemy saw you because you got stuck on a .05inch divot on the ground when trying to creep by or an enemy saw you because he teleported in while you were headbutting a safe, that's a problem with the game. Because of these reasons, as well as the ultimately repetitive gameplay, I recommend doing what I did and getting this on sale. Don't expect something in the same vein as Splinter Cell: Chaos Theory, though.

Overall an alright game, it's rough around the edges but still pretty good overall.
You should know however, some patches made within the last few years have made some late-game houses seriously mechanically broken.

The biggest issue is the ability for tenants to detect if a normally locked interactable is unlocked, (eg. if a door is normally supposed to be locked, they'll call police instantly if they see it's unlocked). This gives the "Burglary Discovered by Tenant" effect, likely ending your attempt if a police officer finds you, or giving a large XP reduction even if you manage to hide or escape.

The way you're supposed to engage with this mechanic is by re-locking doors/windows/etc. behind you so there's nothing unlocked to be detected. This does work, but only for doors and windows that can be lock-picked.

Any door or other interactable that requires hacking tools cannot be re-locked.

This means, for many of the mid-late game houses, it's basically impossible to properly use stealth (and earn the stealth XP bonus) since you're guaranteed to be detected at least once from 24/7 guards that regularly patrol near or through doors that must be hacked to progress.

For an oversight this massive and for how much it harms the experience, I cannot recommend this game in its current state.

At first look, when I saw this game on Steam, it honestly looked like one of those asset flip games.  You know, the kind that BigFry shits on in his YouTube videos.  The type of games where the developer grabbed a few blueprints, mixed in some assets, and made it work [i]just[/i] well enough to edit a trailer out of it.  So I saw the game on Steam awhile ago, thought it looked cool, but never pulled the trigger because the graphics didn't really do it justice.  None of my friends seemed to be playing it, so I didn't wanna take any chances and moved on.  Then I saw a VTuber (don't judge me!) playing it.  The actual gameplay looked fun so I grabbed it, and so far I've thrown about 10 hours into the game in a matter of days.  It's that good.

Lots of games have cool mechanics, but they introduce them in a way that I frankly don't have the patience for.  Tutorials are boring and forced, but Thief Sim does a great job of simply guiding you along your first missions with some hints and stuff and it gets you going without getting in the way.  After you understand the mechanics of the game, or even before if you want... it's all free-roam GTA style.  You can break into any house you want, steal stuff... or not. What surprised me is every time I felt like I was nearing the end of the game, and I already felt like I got my money's worth... it would drop some big new thing on me to explore.  First it was the ability to steal cars from peoples garages.  Then it was a whole new neighborhood.  Then it was disassembling cars so the the parts can be sold at a higher price.  Disabling home security systems, and so on.  This game is very well thought out and keeps giving surprises.

I usually don't review games before I finish them, but I wanted to recommend this game while it's still on sale.  Knowing what I know now, it's totally worth $20... but I think $20 puts it out of the range of impulse buys for most people, me included.

You know that conversation-starter question you hear at parties? There's a few but there's one that sticks out in my mind, "If you could commit any crime without any consequences, what would it be?" or some variation of "If you could get away with anything..." and "What would you do during The Purge?" My answer is always the same: Straight up burglary. It's been a fantasy of mine that might have spawned, as some other reviewer mentioned, during the Burglary minigame in GTA: San Andreas. Ever since I've focused myself on stealthy gameplay and gravitated towards franchises like Splinter Cell, Assassin's Creed, and typically focus on rogue types in Elder Scrolls.

This game scratches and itch in a way I can barely describe. I’m not used to Simulators as they typically feel bare-bones and gimmicky, and I am simply not good at many. Even in city builders, I tend to turn on infinite money and just start building for aesthetics. However this game has damn near everything I’d want in a burglary simulator.

There’s actually casing a house and peaking in windows to figure out where people go during which hours. I like how it only gives you a few hour block of scheduling which forces a few visits to really get someone’s schedule down. During one invasion on a three-floor home, I had about 80% of both tenant’s schedule down but I did find out that one of the people remains home at all times. However with most of her schedule down I was able to duck and weave, and discovered audio ranges. I smashed a car window a full floor above her and while I did get the “Tenant heard noise” message, she wasn’t in a hurry to find the source and got a very nice payout from doing so. Of course, I nicked a bunch of stuff on the way out.

The leveling system is fun to play around with, though I wish the backback came at a boosted amount. In the beginning I can only carry a couple of candlesticks, a chessboard and maybe a hard drive or two. I wish my outings were more bountiful as I can do a lot in one trip if the game allowed me. You get a box in your car that can hold a few things if you’re doing multiple hits, and I did discover on accident that my car can actually hold multiple ‘large’ items. One time I managed to get a TV and two paintings before hauling my tail into a very large experience and money payout. I just wish I could do even more, but eventually I will be able to do so.

I was honestly very surprised with how open ended the game quickly became. After a few initial tutorial “missions” given by some guy named Vinny over your cellphone, the neighborhood becomes your playground. I can come and go as I pleased and I certainly needed to due to my small backpack that I already mentioned. You might have a mission to break someone’s toilet, but you can just as easily go to your computer and pick several other similar missions like stealing a painting or breaking some windows. Each and every one are useful as it may get you closer to a tenant and ultimately learn more about their schedule, which is eternally useful.

I do feel this game needs a heavy dose of home decoration to help detract from the bare-bones feel, in the same vein as House Flipper. Typically every house is perfectly clean with hardly any clutter to speak of, almost as if every single tenant moved in at the same time. I just wish the places looked more lived-in.

I also feel the mechanics could stand to be more nuanced. “Nuance” is a word that has popped up for this game in other reviews and while some complexities to rear their head to my surprise (I tosses a TV out the window a while before a tenant would leave for work or whatever and he immediately recognized he own stolen television chilling out on his driveway, and thus an alert was sound), I still believe there’s a lot to be desired. The AI is rather silly at times, passerbys will be suspicious of you just by... existing. Apparently “shady” is doing literally anything at all. I personally have no clue what kind of televisions any of my neighbors have so if I saw a bloke loading one into a car I’d assume they’re selling it or upgrading, my mind doesn’t immediately go to “someone’s getting burgled!” and it would have been nice if the street-going AI had more going for them.

Essentially this feels like a core of a game I wish could acquire a higher budget or publisher. While I’m having a lot of fun with it, I just wish there was... more of it. Which hardly sounds like a complaint, but I hope they either update with ferocity or at least start working on a second one so they can expand everything they’ve laid out here. It’s a damn fine start.

Sure! Here's a long, detailed review of Thief Simulator, covering gameplay, mechanics, visuals, pros, cons, and overall impressions:

Game Review: Thief Simulator
Platforms: PC, Nintendo Switch, PS4 | Developer: Noble Muffins | Publisher: PlayWay S.A.

Rating: 7.5/10

When you hear the title Thief Simulator, your first thought might be that it’s just another quirky sandbox title in the growing niche of job-based simulators. But this one has a unique hook — stepping into the shadows as a burglar and living the life of a career criminal in a semi-open world. It’s a game that’s rough around the edges but surprisingly deep and engaging once you get into the groove.
🎮 Gameplay & Mechanics

At its core, Thief Simulator is about learning the ropes of burglary: casing houses, studying routines, disabling security systems, and making clean getaways. You start small — stealing toasters and old TVs — but eventually, you’re breaking into high-security mansions using advanced tools and skills. The game does a great job of gradually escalating your capabilities through a skill tree, making you feel like a real professional over time.

The game blends stealth, strategy, and puzzle-solving. There’s an open-world feel, although it’s more like a series of large sandbox maps. You can explore neighborhoods, observe patterns (like when people leave the house or go to sleep), and plan your heists accordingly.

It even includes elements like:

    Lockpicking (with several mini-games depending on lock type)

    Hacking electronics and alarms

    Selling loot on the black market

    Pawning items or disassembling them for parts

    Buying burglary tools like glass cutters, jammers, and hacking laptops

There’s also a mission system, with jobs coming in via a dark web-like app on your in-game phone. You’re sometimes asked to retrieve specific items, plant bugs, or just vandalize a property. It adds variety and structure to the otherwise open-ended gameplay.
🔍 Stealth and Strategy

This isn’t a run-and-gun kind of game. If you’re spotted, neighbors call the police, and you’ll need to make a quick escape — either by foot or by car. Getting caught results in losing stolen goods and progress, so planning is key.

The most enjoyable moments come when you’re slowly sneaking through a well-guarded home, ducking under windows and timing your moves between patrols or homeowner routines. There’s a real satisfaction in pulling off a big score without being seen.
🧰 Progression and Tools

As you level up, the tools at your disposal become more elaborate and fun to use. Early-game burglaries are mostly about slipping in when no one’s home, but late-game missions involve surveillance cameras, alarm systems, keycard access, and security guards. It starts to feel like a low-budget Hitman or Payday, which is meant as a compliment.

There’s also a decent amount of customization. You can improve your skills in stealth, agility, hacking, and lockpicking. These upgrades feel meaningful and let you approach situations differently — do you want to climb into a second-story window, or jimmy the front door?
🎨 Graphics & Presentation

Visually, Thief Simulator isn’t going to win any awards. The graphics are serviceable but dated, with environments that feel a bit stiff and NPCs that look robotic. However, the visual style gets the job done — houses are varied enough to keep you interested, and interiors are filled with tons of lootable items.

The UI is functional but not especially elegant. Some menus can feel clunky, especially when trying to manage inventory or use specific tools. But once you learn the ropes, it’s easy to get around.
🔊 Sound Design & Atmosphere

Sound plays a crucial role. Footsteps, doors creaking, alarms — these audio cues are essential when planning your move or reacting to a surprise. While the voice acting is minimal (and often forgettable), the ambient sounds are solid and add tension during a break-in.

The music is mostly forgettable, but that works in the game's favor — it doesn’t distract from the high-stakes silence of sneaking around a dark house.
👍 What Works Well

    Immersive burglary mechanics: The core gameplay loop is fun, especially once you get better tools and start pulling off bigger jobs.

    Open-ended approach: You’re free to plan and execute heists however you like.

    Progression feels rewarding: New tools and skills genuinely open up new playstyles.

    Surprisingly realistic elements: Like selling items, disassembling electronics, or scouting routines.

👎 What Doesn’t Work

    Repetitive missions: While there’s variety early on, some tasks start to feel similar.

    Clunky controls/UI: Tool switching and certain interactions aren’t as smooth as they should be.

    AI can be janky: NPC behavior is sometimes unpredictable or unrealistic.

    Visuals are underwhelming: The game looks like something from 2012, though it runs well.

🧠 Final Thoughts

Thief Simulator is a flawed but charming experience. It’s not polished, and it certainly doesn’t match the production quality of bigger titles, but it does offer something unique — a sandbox-style game where patience, planning, and stealth are rewarded. For players who enjoy stealth mechanics, breaking and entering with a bit of strategy, and some emergent gameplay, this game scratches a niche itch.

It’s especially fun in short bursts, or as a “main heist and chill” kind of game. And while it won’t blow your mind, it’s got that “just one more job” hook that keeps you sneaking back in.

Verdict: If you're looking for an offbeat simulator with criminal flair, Thief Simulator is worth a steal — even if it’s not the cleanest job in the game.

Defintely a fun game to me. I may be biased since I always wanted a game that focuses on burglary above all. Not the Thief series, not Dishonored - both of them amazing series and wonderful at what they do - but simply a game about breaking into people's houses and clearing them out.
This game is all about that.

Now before I get any further, I will reccommend one thing. Enable hard mode. Everything is much more intense when you don't get a minimap or person radar, and you have to rely more on your instincts. Also do yourself a favor and avoid buying tenant information, instead just scope the place out. Much more immersive that way.

Gameplay wise it's fairly straightforward. Scope out the place, mark your routes of entry, and once the time comes, get in and go about your business. Be sure to be quick about it, yet still quiet if the tenants are asleep or even up and awake, and sometimes come back more than once if say, you spot something you couldn't snag on the first visit.
The map is open world, and limitations from missing tools aside, you can hit up any place you want. There are story missions that mainly consist of "steal X" or "break X" as far as I have played, and you are able to take on other hit jobs for houses to do additional objectives.
Furthermore, the black market allows you to sell certain items - or groups of items - for a bit of extra money, rewarding keeping an eye on it.

Graphically the game definitely suffices, it looks good enough in my eyes, and has no graphics issues I can see, except from a rather weak AA algorhythm that doesn't really reduce the jaggies all htat much. But from a performance standpoint, no complaints here.

Gameplay wise, I would comment on three aspects I found to be a bit negative. One, the AI spotting is often instant, I would prefer a system a bit more payday oriented. Two, hiding is a bit too brainless and easy, and should be implemented a little better. And lastly, even at night houses are bright enough from ambient light so as to not necessitate a flashlight whatsoever, maybe this changes later, but for now I flat out don't need it. I would love some changes there to make night time burglaries a bit more intense.

Now to address some complaints other people had:
- Quick time passage: A bit odd but I like it, makes it so that you have to move quickly to capitalize on people being out of the house, and puts an element of tension on you breaking in, putting you under pressure. Of course you can always find out tenant routines and instead break in while they are sleeping, giving you much more time, but also greater risk and a need to move quietly.
- Tight inventory/car inventory: Once again a limiting factor, forcing you to choose valuable items and remember what fetches a good price or is wanted on Blackbay, rather than simply mashing E on everything that comes your way, I like it. One suggestion however, I would love to be able to get a different car eventually, perhaps even acquire and convert a stolen vehicle for one extra large item slot. That would be just about perfect.

All in all a game that in my eyes, is worth the price, and offers a lot of fun. And once more my reccomendation, play it in hard mode, its better!
